title: What is the small-files problem in Spark — too many tiny output files (common after streaming writes or high-cardinality `partitionBy`) cause excessive metadata overhead, slow file listing, and task scheduling overhead — and how do you fix it (coalesce before write, `maxRecordsPerFile`, periodic compaction, Delta Lake `OPTIMIZE`)?
topicTitle: What is the small-files problem in Spark

s1_definition.profdef: The small-files problem is a performance degradation that occurs when a dataset is stored as a very large number of tiny files instead of a smaller number of appropriately sized files. It arises commonly from streaming writes that emit a few records per micro-batch, from high-cardinality partitionBy that creates millions of directories each with a sliver of data, and from over-partitioned jobs where each task writes its own small file. The consequences are excessive metadata overhead on the file system or object store, slow file listing when planning a read, and task scheduling overhead because Spark creates one task per file. Fixes include coalescing before writing, bounding file size with maxRecordsPerFile, running periodic compaction jobs, and using a table format's maintenance like Delta Lake OPTIMIZE to rewrite small files into larger ones.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India imagine filing each transaction slip in its own separate envelope in a giant cabinet. Finding and processing a day's slips now means opening millions of envelopes — the opening and listing of envelopes takes far longer than reading the slips themselves. The small-files problem is exactly this: too many tiny files means the bank spends its time on file bookkeeping instead of on the data. The fix is to batch many slips into a sensibly sized folder (larger files), cap how many slips go in each folder, and periodically consolidate scattered single-slip envelopes into proper folders (compaction / OPTIMIZE).
s1_definition.oneliner: Too many tiny files cause metadata, listing, and scheduling overhead; fix it with coalesce before write, maxRecordsPerFile, periodic compaction, or Delta Lake OPTIMIZE to produce fewer, right-sized files.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The small-files problem is a performance degradation that occurs when a dataset is stored as a very large number of tiny files instead of a smaller number of appropriately sized files. It arises commonly from streaming writes that emit a few records per micro-batch, from high-cardinality partitionBy that creates millions of directories each with a sliver of data, and from over-partitioned jobs where each task writes its own small file. The consequences are excessive metadata overhead on the file system or object store, slow file listing when planning a read, and task scheduling overhead because Spark creates one task per file. Fixes include coalescing before writing, bounding file size with maxRecordsPerFile, running periodic compaction jobs, and using a table format's maintenance like Delta Lake OPTIMIZE to rewrite small files into larger ones.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India imagine filing each transaction slip in its own separate envelope in a giant cabinet. Finding and processing a day's slips now means opening millions of envelopes — the opening and listing of envelopes takes far longer than reading the slips themselves. The small-files problem is exactly this: too many tiny files means the bank spends its time on file bookkeeping instead of on the data. The fix is to batch many slips into a sensibly sized folder (larger files), cap how many slips go in each folder, and periodically consolidate scattered single-slip envelopes into proper folders (compaction / OPTIMIZE).

**One line to remember:** Too many tiny files cause metadata, listing, and scheduling overhead; fix it with coalesce before write, maxRecordsPerFile, periodic compaction, or Delta Lake OPTIMIZE to produce fewer, right-sized files.

sections.s2_technical:
The root causes are a few recurring patterns. Streaming writes are the classic one: a micro-batch every few seconds writes whatever it processed, so a low-volume stream produces thousands of tiny files per hour. High-cardinality partitionBy is another: partitioning by a near-unique column like account id or transaction id creates a directory per value, each holding almost nothing, multiplying file count. Over-partitioning in batch jobs is a third: if a DataFrame has far more partitions than needed at write time, each partition becomes a separate output file regardless of how little data it holds.

The consequences compound at scale. Every file is an entry the metastore or object store must track, so metadata grows large and operations on it slow down. Before a read, Spark lists the files to plan the job, and listing millions of files — especially on object stores like S3 where listing is a relatively expensive API — can take minutes before any data is read. Then Spark creates one task per file, so a read of a million tiny files schedules a million tasks, and the per-task overhead dwarfs the actual work, wasting cluster time and driver memory on task bookkeeping. The ideal file size is usually in the range of roughly 128 megabytes to 1 gigabyte, aligned with block and row-group sizes.

The write-time fixes reduce how many files are produced. Coalescing or repartitioning before the write controls the number of output files: coalesce(n) reduces partitions without a shuffle to produce about n files, while repartition(n) or repartition by the partition column rebalances to produce evenly sized files. For partitioned writes, repartitioning by the partition column before writing ensures each partition directory gets one file per writer rather than many. The maxRecordsPerFile option caps how many records go into a single file, which bounds file size on the upper end and, combined with sensible partition counts, keeps files in the healthy range.

The maintenance fixes consolidate files after the fact. For streaming and append-heavy tables, you run periodic compaction jobs that read the many small files of a partition and rewrite them as a few large ones. Lakehouse table formats make this a first-class operation: Delta Lake provides OPTIMIZE, which compacts small files into larger ones and can Z-order for data skipping, and Iceberg and Hudi have equivalent compaction. These run as scheduled maintenance so the live write path stays simple while the read path benefits from compacted files. A senior-level nuance is the tension between streaming latency and file size: writing less frequently produces larger files but adds latency, so you either accept small files from the stream and compact later, or you tune trigger intervals and use maxRecordsPerFile to strike a balance. The mature approach is to design the write path to avoid high-cardinality partitionBy, coalesce to a target file count before batch writes, and schedule compaction or OPTIMIZE for streaming tables, rather than discovering the problem only when reads mysteriously take minutes to plan.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India streams transactions and writes every thirty seconds, producing thousands of tiny Parquet files a day. Reads of the day's data spend minutes just listing files. Scheduled compaction rewrites them into large files.

Problem 2 — A batch job mistakenly partitions by transaction id, a near-unique column, creating millions of one-row directories. Removing that partitionBy and partitioning by date instead fixes the explosion.

Problem 3 — A batch write has two hundred partitions but only a little data, producing two hundred small files. Coalescing to a handful of partitions before writing produces right-sized files.

The demo models a file-layout analyzer that, given a write's record count, partition count, and partitioning column cardinality, estimates the resulting file count and average file size, flags a small-files problem, and recommends coalesce, dropping high-cardinality partitionBy, maxRecordsPerFile, or compaction.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/spark-small-files-demo-1.0.0.jar com.bank.spark.SmallFilesDemo

# Real fixes:
# df.coalesce(8).write.parquet(path)                      # fewer files
# df.write.option("maxRecordsPerFile",1000000).parquet(path)
# -- Delta Lake maintenance:
# OPTIMIZE bank.transactions WHERE date >= '2026-10-01';
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: three write plans — partitioning by transaction id with a million distinct values, an over-partitioned batch with two hundred Spark partitions for little data, and a healthy write by date coalesced to eight partitions over thirty dates.

Step 1: The partition-by-txnid plan is analyzed. Estimated files equal four partitions times one million directories, an enormous count, with a tiny average size far below the healthy threshold. The analyzer flags high-cardinality partitionBy and recommends dropping it, partitioning by date, and using maxRecordsPerFile.

Step 2: The over-partitioned-batch plan is analyzed. One directory times two hundred partitions gives two hundred small files for only half a million records, below the healthy size. The analyzer recommends coalescing before write and scheduling compaction or Delta OPTIMIZE.

Step 3: The healthy-by-date plan is analyzed. Eight partitions times thirty date directories gives two hundred forty files for a large dataset, so the average file size is well above the healthy threshold, and the analyzer reports it as healthy.

Step 4: The demo logs each plan's estimated file count, average size, and recommendation, showing how the same healthy-size rule distinguishes a problem layout from a good one.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The small-files problem is when a dataset ends up stored as a huge number of tiny files instead of fewer, right-sized ones, and it degrades performance in three ways: excessive metadata the metastore or object store must track, slow file listing during read planning — which on object stores like S3 can take minutes before any data is read — and task scheduling overhead because Spark creates one task per file, so a million tiny files means a million tasks whose overhead dwarfs the real work. The healthy file size is usually in the range of roughly 128 megabytes to a gigabyte.

The common causes are specific and recognizable. Streaming writes emit a few records per micro-batch, so a low-volume stream produces thousands of tiny files per hour. High-cardinality partitionBy — partitioning by a near-unique column like account id or transaction id — creates a directory per value, each with almost nothing, exploding the file count. Over-partitioned batch jobs write one small file per excess partition. The fixes map to these: coalesce or repartition before the write to control the number of output files, repartition by the partition column so each directory gets one file per writer, bound file size with maxRecordsPerFile, and avoid high-cardinality partitionBy by partitioning on something low-cardinality like date. For append-heavy and streaming tables you run periodic compaction, and lakehouse formats make this first-class with Delta Lake OPTIMIZE or the Iceberg and Hudi equivalents.

At the National Bank of India our streaming transaction table wrote every thirty seconds and accumulated thousands of small Parquet files a day, until reads of the day's data started spending minutes just listing files; we fixed it by scheduling a nightly Delta OPTIMIZE that compacted each partition into a few large files, which cut read planning dramatically. We also caught a batch job that had mistakenly partitioned by transaction id, creating millions of one-row directories, and fixed it by partitioning on date and coalescing before the write. The design rule I give in interviews is to avoid high-cardinality partitionBy, coalesce to a target file count before batch writes, bound file size with maxRecordsPerFile, and schedule compaction or OPTIMIZE for streaming tables — so you prevent the problem at the write path rather than discovering it when reads mysteriously slow down.
